📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

It was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

It has been revealed that this latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

Aston Villa make a mistake at the back and Lamine Yamal makes them pay inside 10 minutes ⚡ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/1IcWOPMJlt.

Recent findings suggest that at the heart of Barcelona’s victory was Lamine Yamal, their outstanding jewel from the academy. The 19-year-old became the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history, eclipsing the record of 13 he previously shared with Kylian Mbappé, with the opening goal.

Yamal was orchestrating everything from the pace of the match to the volume of the supporters, at one point imploring them to raise the noise in the first half with both arms aloft.

There was also another impressive performance from England international Anthony Gordon and Raphinha, who dedicated his two goals to the memory of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife forward, who died on Tuesday.

With that tragedy fresh in the minds and the Nou Camp under construction, it was a peculiar atmosphere at times.

Sources indicate that the defeat marked the end of Villa’s 100 per cent record in the competition, with a tough test away at Galatasaray up next before they host PSG in December. They remain high up in the table and have often displayed a propensity to bounce back quickly from defeats.

Recent findings suggest that emery noted: “We are in a process and this was a very good test against a team like Barcelona. We are not at the level we want to achieve but there are a lot of experiences for us to take. Overall, we are competing fantastically in the Champions League and there is still work to do.

Sources indicate that “Over the process we’ve had here, we have made mistakes but then overcame them. We accept this defeat but take a lot of information from it.”.

Nine years have passed since Emery’s last visit in this competition and time has not proved a great healer.

In a recent development, then in charge of PSG, Emery witnessed his team surrender a 4-0 first-leg lead to lose 6-5 on aggregate. Any matches where he is involved at the Nou Camp will revive memories of that remarkable comeback. He must have feared a repeat of more pain when Yamal, making his 37th Champions League appearance, rewarded Barcelona’s early pressure.

Recent findings suggest that villa’s defending needed to be as close to perfect as possible, but they were exposed after a poor error of judgment from Gomes. Under pressure from Barcelona’s attackers, Gomes panicked and played a blind pass into the path of Yamal, who bent his left-footed shot into the corner.

Sources indicate that that mistake could have threatened to damage confidence but Villa did respond. Matty Cash’s half-volley from inside the penalty area was only a few inches wide, while Johan Manzambi side-footed wide of the goal after a quick break down the right from Nicolas Jackson.

With Andreas Christensen, Eric García, Xavi Espart and Jules Koundé all absent here, Barcelona’s defence did appear vulnerable. Jackson was targeting the flanks and having his more dangerous moments challenging their high line. Emery paced his technical area, imploring his players to remain focused.

Industry observers note that yet Barcelona’s forward three were always a threat and they increased their lead eight minutes into the second half. Raphinha was given too much room to turn in the penalty area and his shot took a heavy deflection off the heel of Pau Torres to find the bottom corner. Emery was furious, appearing to raise his fist in the air at another poor goal conceded.

Raphinha doubles Barcelona's lead with his 18th goal of the season! 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/NzFPYVzDuj.

Barcelona added a third goal with Raphinha converting from close range after a sublime pass from João Cancelo.

According to recent reports, raphinha dedicated his goals to De Miguel, who died on Tuesday after sustaining serious injuries during a match the previous night. He noted: “Tonight I don’t want to talk about football. I want to send a lot of strength to Jesus de Miguel’s family.

Sources indicate that “May he rest in peace. In the end, this can happen to anyone. The truth is that it’s very tough. When we saw the news this morning, it was complicated. I’m incredibly shocked and sad. In the end, you go to play a match, and the same thing could happen to you. From myself, from the club, we want to send a lot of strength to his family.”.

Villa did continue to fight for a consolation, with substitute Leon Goretzka heading against the post and their 3,000 travelling fans continued to sing in the rain after the final whistle.

This was the first encounter between the two clubs since the European Super Cup Final in January 1983, and yet another reminder of the upward trajectory under Emery.

"His numbers are staggering." 🤯 Joe Cole on Raphinha after he scored his 19th goal of the season in Barcelona's 3-0 win over Aston Villa ⭐ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOUq1QaYKE.

Industry observers note that “When you come to places like this, you need to start well and weather the storm, and we did not do this. When you play against teams like Barcelona, you do not get a second chance. There are lessons to be learnt. Our final pass let us down tonight. Barcelona made the right decisions at the right times. The manager spoke about being clinical in important moments in the game. We knew what we were coming up against. In order for us to get all three points we needed to be a lot better. I think we are competitive against teams at this level and we have shown that. We have shown we can make them sweat and cause them problems.”.

It has been revealed that aston Villa have made the trip over to Spain to take on Barcelona in the Champions League on matchday four. These teams last met all the way back in 1983, when they met in the European Super Cup. Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

According to recent reports, “In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery mentioned. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

Sources indicate that “[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”.

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

Industry observers note that “We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which demonstrated it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Substitute Carlos Espí struck late as Real Madrid came from behind to beat Celta Vigo 2-1 at the Santiago Bernabéu. The result keeps Madrid firmly in the title race with Barcelona.

The victory over Celta on Saturday 21 November 2026 was Madrid’s ninth in a row. It also kept their 100% home record this season intact.

Recent findings suggest that the winner began with a Vinícius Júnior cross. Espí headed it, Celta goalkeeper Ionuț Radu saved, and the striker scored from the rebound in the six-yard box. He had been on the pitch for only a few minutes.

It has been revealed that espí had played only 44 minutes of LaLiga football this season before kick-off, according to ESPN. All three of his league goals have now won games, against Espanyol, Elche and Celta. He also scored in the 4-3 Champions League comeback win at Roma. The goal was his fourth of the season, the club remarked.

Sources indicate that espí called his first goal in front of the Bernabéu crowd his most special for the club. José Mourinho described him as a pure penalty-box striker. The coach added that football history has many players like him who decide games without playing many minutes.

According to recent reports, pablo Durán gave Celta a sixth-minute lead from a Williot Swedberg pass. Kylian Mbappé then missed a penalty in the 39th minute, and the visitors led 1-0 at the break.

Sources indicate that mourinho had started Vinícius and Federico Valverde on the bench. He sent them on with Marc Cucurella in the second half to chase the game. Thibaut Courtois kept Madrid in it with a strong low save from a long-range Durán shot in the 65th minute. A minute later, Jude Bellingham equalised from an Mbappé assist.

The figures show how one-sided the contest was. Madrid had 24 shots to Celta’s 8 and an expected goals total of 3.8 against 1.52. Radu made five saves, and the hosts held 64% of possession.

Celta coach Claudio Giráldez said Madrid’s substitutes had decided the game. He pointed out that he had started six academy graduates. Many of his players were appearing at the Bernabéu for the first time. Giráldez replaced Hugo Álvarez with Ferran Jutglà at half-time and sent on Iago Aspas for Durán in the 76th minute. Celta are 13th on 13 points.

Barcelona still top the table on goal difference, 35 to 22. They can move clear again when they host Villarreal on Sunday 22 November.

Recent findings suggest that in the LaLiga scoring chart, Mbappé is second with 13 goals. Barcelona’s Raphinha leads on 15.

Earlier on Saturday, Rafael Nadal was elected to Real Madrid’s board of directors at an Extraordinary General Assembly at Ciudad Real Madrid. Later, he watched the game from the stands and was visibly emotional.

Sources indicate that celta host Bournemouth in the Europa League at Balaídos on Thursday 26 November, with 3 points from four games. Madrid face PSV in the Champions League at the Bernabéu on Tuesday 24 November at 20:00 UTC. I've been to all 92 grounds in the Premier League and Football League and this is my definitive ranking from worst to best - where does YOUR club end up?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 91 min read (18104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~91 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Industry observers note that some grounds are beautiful.
  • But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.

Industry observers note that some grounds are beautiful. Some grounds are not so beautiful. Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game. And some leave you feeling like you're on the periphery.

But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.

On April 1, 2025, I made the trip to Harrogate Town’s Exercise Stadium and first fulfilled the quest of a lifetime by completing the set of all 92 English Football League grounds for Daily Mail Sport. But then Everton moved away from Goodison Park and into a stunning latest stadium on the banks of the River Mersey.

Recent findings suggest that I was one short again but on February 23, 2026, I got back up to 92 by going to Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch Everton versus Manchester United. Then, in November, with York City being promoted (alongside Rochdale, whose ground I had ticked off decades ago), I made the trip to the LNER Stadium to make the 92 whole again.

In a recent development, I won’t give too much away just yet, but why are grounds like AFC Wimbledon and Exeter City in my top 20? What about Anfield, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge? Where does Everton’s dazzling upcoming home rank? Where is the best grub in the Premier League and where did Tyson Fury once threaten to have my jaw broken?

In a recent development, this is my love letter to English football. Read on to find out who comes out on top, where your team ranks and everything else in between – then let me know what you think of my guide to the 92 grounds of England.

Division: Championship Opened: 1993 Capacity: 19,369.

Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir.

Industry observers note that I’ve been banned from The Den for the last 20 months, in a professional capacity anyway. I could still go in a personal capacity but, on balance, I think I’d rather not.

The Daily Mail has been told that our reporters are not welcome at the club because we had the temerity to report on the horrendous challenge by Millwall goalkeeper Liam Roberts on Crystal Palace’s Jean-Philippe Mateta during the FA Cup tie at Selhurst Park in March last year, which left the French striker requiring 25 stitches in his left ear.

In a recent development, let’s be honest about this: there are worse places to be banned from. Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir. You don’t have to be a racist, misogynistic, homophobic bloke with anger complications and a penchant for tragedy-chanting to feel at home at The Den. But it helps.

And, yes, I know Millwall are trying to rebrand themselves as a ‘family club’ now and the odd Tarquin and Tabitha stray across the county lines from Blackheath and Clapham to keep it real but that just makes The Den experience even worse.

The last time I went as a supporter was 16 years ago to watch Stockport County play there and the walk from South Bermondsey station to the away turnstiles was an eye-opener.

Recent findings suggest that not that there were any problems: even at Millwall, football has moved on since the 70s. But this still felt deeply dystopian: for their own safety, away fans walk to the ground through a long wire mesh cage that seems to have no end. It felt like embarking on a tour of Jurassic Park: you know that if the fences fail, the dinosaurs are going to take a run at you.

Sources indicate that inside the ground, which is modern and neat and relatively characterless, the level of hatred for visiting supporters feels unusually visceral. It’s loud. I’ll give it that. It’s primeval. It’s unreconstructed, which can be a good thing, too, and it breeds a sense of togetherness.

Industry observers note that if medievalism is your thing, you’re in for a treat. If not, give it a miss.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 30,303.

I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons, for that matter.

Sources indicate that I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons themselves for that matter.

Industry observers note that the club was born under a bad sign when it was jemmied out of Wimbledon and moved to Milton Keynes in 2003 and it has never been able to shake the stigma since. The stadium fits the club.

It is a soulless, faceless, gloomy place. More than that, there is something rather forbidding about it. Its 30,000 capacity is too big for the club it hosts and, apart from the joys of the local KFC and McDonald’s, there is little to recommend in its immediate surrounds. Its black seats lend it a sinister air, too.

It’s the kind of stadium only its mother could love. And it doesn’t have a mother. Unless you want to do the 92, give it a miss.

90. Kassam Stadium, Oxford United.

Division: League One Opened: 2001 Capacity: 12,537.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate.

I feel ashamed to say it, given that it is my local club, but the best experience I’ve had at the Kassam Stadium was getting my Covid jab there during the pandemic.

When they moved, around the turn of the century, abandoning the chaotic charm of the Manor Ground in Headington and swapping it for an isolated plateau outside the city, they only completed three sides, abandoning the fourth because of rising costs.

A particularly bitter wind blows in off the car park behind one of the goals and, from the main stand – in fact, from every stand – there is a magnificent and uninterrupted view of the Frankie and Benny's in the mini retail park that abuts the ground.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, too, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate given they have endured a generation of being stuck here. Firoz Kassam still owns the stadium but not the club. That kind of separation always spells trouble.

It has been revealed that oxford are hoping to move to a upcoming stadium to the north of the city in a couple of years’ time. It can’t come soon enough.

89. London Stadium, West Ham United.

Division: Championship Opened: 2012 Capacity: 62,500.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground.

Sources indicate that I don’t even like calling it the London Stadium. It’s the Olympic Stadium, but it suited the David Sullivan-Karren Brady rebrand of the club to give it the capital’s name.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground. It’s also a monument to much that is wrong with the upper reaches of the English game: a surrender of identity and tradition as collateral damage in the owners’ pursuit of profit.

Walking to it, sadly, feels a bit like walking through a wasteland and its odd configuration inside harms the atmosphere even though the fans are right up there with the best in the country. The old stadium at Upton Park was intimate and raucous and intimidating. The London Stadium is nothing like that.

The owners spent a lot of time congratulating themselves on the deal they did to move to the new ground: they’re the archetypes of football owners who know the price of everything and the value of nothing.

Industry observers note that 88. Hillsborough, Sheffield Wednesday.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 34,835.

It is hard to get past Hillsborough's association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and the betrayal of supporters.

I used to think of Hillsborough as one of the cathedrals of the English game but since the disaster that claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans in 1989, it is hard to get past its association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and betrayal of supporters.

I know, obviously, that this would punish Wednesday fans who do not deserve to be punished for something that had nothing to do with them but Hillsborough, and its Leppings Lane End in particular, has such a cursed legacy that part of me thinks it should have been demolished and that the club should have moved elsewhere.

Even in the last couple of years, fans of Newcastle United and Leeds United have reported serious safety concerns in the Leppings Lane End.

I recognise the flaws in my argument about demolishing the stadium, or part of it, and the emotions it provokes on all sides so perhaps it’s just enough to say I’ll never feel the same about the stadium as I once did.

Visiting it now feels like an intrusion.

87. Sixfields, Northampton Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1994 Capacity: 8,203.

Sixfields is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sixfields is a blighted stadium.

It is a soulless ground anyway but its challenges have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

In a recent development, it has the same kind of deracinated feel as so many of the latest-build stadia pushed to the peripheries of towns. Its supporters deserve a lot better.

86. Broadfield Stadium, Crawley Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1997 Capacity: 5,907.

If you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two.

Not an awful lot to relish about the Broadfield Stadium, to be honest.

Decent fans, of course, just like at every club, but Crawley Town’s home is a bit of a modern monstrosity, next to a roundabout outside town on the A23.

Recent findings suggest that if you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two. I had fun when I visited because I was in the away end with Stockport fans but I’m not in any hurry to go back.

Football at the CBS Arena feels like it is in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless.

When it was called the Ricoh Arena, I had no interest in visiting what is now the Coventry Building Society Arena because it felt like a symbol of the callous way in which fans of the club were being treated by SISU, the hedge fund that owned it at the time.

It has been revealed that but SISU sold up in the end and I went along a few years back to see Coventry dismantle Wayne Rooney’s Birmingham City. Recent findings suggest that 84. JobServe Community Stadium, Colchester United.

This stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is rather a bleak place to watch football.

The staff at the club are great, the stewards are friendly, there's plenty of parking, there's a Wendy's next door and the home fans, largely arranged in a stand behind one of the goals, make a superb first of creating an atmosphere.

But this stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is still rather a bleak place to watch football.

It probably didn’t help that I went on a dank March night when a wispy fog lingered in the dim floodlight glare but there was something ethereally gloomy about the JobServe Community Stadium.

The empty corridors and the cavernous suites lent it a slight feel of the Overlook Hotel on the inside. On the outside, the four corners of the stadium are open, which makes for especially bitter nights in the winter.

Home is home and there was still plenty of drama and passion in Colchester’s 1-0 victory over Chesterfield – the match I saw – but it came despite the stadium, not because of it.

The Bescot was the first of the generation of identikit fresh-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

Division: League One Opened: 1999 Capacity: 25,133.

Division: League Two Opened: 2007 Capacity: 9,875.

Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Gay Meadow, the former home of Shrewsbury Town, was one of the best grounds in our top four divisions.

It might have flooded now and again because of its position on the banks of the River Severn but it was a fine old ground and the tradition of a boatman taking to a coracle to fish wayward shots that cleared the roof of the stand out of the river was one of the most cherished peculiarities in our game.

The Croud Meadow is altogether more prosaic. Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

80. Select Car Leasing Stadium, Reading.

Division: League One Opened: 1998 Capacity: 24,376.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006, when Steve Coppell and Wally Downes were in charge at the Madejski Stadium.

People called it the Mad Stad back then and I remember Neil Warnock telling me about being chased to his car outside the main entrance when he was manager of Sheffield United.

And Wally took a swing at me at a Football Writers’ Association dinner a couple of years later.

Anyway, I’ve made up with Stephen Hunt, who was one of the players involved in the tumult against Chelsea, and with Downes since then.

Even if the Mad Stad doesn’t have an awful lot of personality, I have only respect for the Reading fans who endured so much under the ownership of Dai Yongge and fought for their club.

Sources indicate that 79. Pride Park Stadium, Derby County.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 32,956.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost character because the fans just merge into one.

Pride Park is the standard-bearer, sadly, for what is lacking in many of the new generation of English football stadia.

English football grounds should be about the North Bank and the Stretford End and the Kop and the Gallowgate End and the Shelf.

They’re supposed to be about defined areas that give a stadium character and personality and even rivalry among home fans about who sings loudest.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost that character because the fans just merge into one.

Sources indicate that this is not a criticism of Derby County fans in any way. They still make plenty of noise inside their stadium but the place is not a patch on the Baseball Ground, which witnessed so many momentous days and nights.

Pride Park is bland and featureless, a symbol of its team’s current struggle for identity as it languishes near the foot of the Championship.

In a recent development, 78. Swansea.com Stadium, Swansea City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2003 Capacity: 20,996.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks character but is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

My in-laws used to live in Swansea and when I wasn’t out walking to Worm’s Head at Rhossili or enjoying the delights of Mumbles and the Wales Coast Path, I’d make the occasional pilgrimage to what was left of the Vetch Field.

Recent findings suggest that I stood in the away end there with Manchester United fans in the early 80s but when I visited later in my life, the Vetch was locked up and derelict. If you peered through the gates, you could see small trees and shrubs growing on the pitch.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks the same character, obviously, but it is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

I did a phone interview with Mike Tyson from the press box here a couple of hours before a game once. I couldn’t hear him very well because of various announcements being made over the loud-speaker system and soon, his tone became rather impatient but still, a conversation with Mike Tyson in the press box at Swansea is not easily forgotten.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

According to recent reports, abutting King’s Park and not far from the sea front, it’s a ground that almost manages to feel quaint. But not quite.

It doesn’t feel as though Southampton's St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

It doesn’t feel as though St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of new-builds largely devoid of character.

Sources indicate that 73. King Power Stadium, Leicester City.

Division: League One Opened: 2002 Capacity: 32,259.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans can make plenty of noise but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the newly introduced era of stadia.

One of the few times I was genuinely scared at a football stadium when I was a supporter was during a visit to Leicester City’s former stadium at Filbert Street.

In the crush to get out of the away end at the final whistle, I was lifted off my feet in the surge.

So I’m aware that there are limits to how much one should mourn the passing of that generation of stadia but I still find it hard to warm to arenas like the King Power.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans made plenty of noise in happier times but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the newly introduced generation of stadia.

Even then, it provided me with one of the great memories of the last decade when Andrea Bocelli stood next to Claudio Ranieri and sang Nessun Dorma the game after Leicester had pulled off the shock of the century by winning the Premier League in 2016.

Division: League One Opened: 1961 Capacity: 7,426.

Broadhall Way is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere, and home to a friendly club.

Sources indicate that 71. EV Charger Points Stadium, Cheltenham Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1927 Capacity: 6,923.

EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

It is a high bar in these days when money counts a lot more than heritage and finances are fraught at the wrong end of the EFL, but the EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

We should just stick with Whaddon Road really but it was renamed the Abbey Business Stadium in 2009, then it became The World of Smile Stadium, then the LCI Rail Stadium in 2016–17, then the Jonny-Rocks Stadium in 2018–19, and the Completely-Suzuki Stadium in 2022 and now its current glorious and evocative name.

I hope they got a lot of money for those sponsorships because they make the club look stupid and cheap and rip chunks of its identity away from it.

Again, I know it’s probably not financially viable to do away with them but I hate stadium naming rights. I’d ban them if I could. Football survived for a century without them, so why not now?

It’s a shame because it’s a fine little ground that provides a different focus in a town dominated by horse racing.

Recent findings suggest that 70. LNER Community Stadium, York City.

Division: League Two Opened: 2021 Capacity: 8,500.

According to recent reports, david 'Bumble' Lloyd, England's former cricket coach and a broadcasting legend, is a season-ticket holder at York City. 'A grand stadium,' he mentioned of the ground the club moved to in January 2021 after 90 years at Bootham Crescent.

After York's promotion from the National League last season, it was the only ground of the 92 that I had not visited and I made my first trip there this month for the FA Cup first-round tie against Northampton Town.

The upcoming stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

In a recent development, I don't particularly warm to out-of-town stadiums built next to retail parks but York challenged that perception. Society is changing and town planning is changing. Retail parks are our upcoming high streets and if a club is to be at the heart of a community, there are worse places for it to be than beside a Hotel Chocolat, an M&S Foodhall, a multiplex cinema, a teaching hospital, a leisure centre and a bowling alley.

I'd paid my homage to Bootham Crescent earlier by visiting the housing estate where it once stood. A small part of the main stand and the players' tunnel has been preserved, which is, at least, a nod to the club's heritage but I wish there were more.

The upcoming stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two of the four stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

Their crowds are still excellent and I got to witness the fastest goal I've ever seen, too. York scored after 10 seconds, the quickest goal in FA Cup first-round history, and I walked back to my car, past the Aldi, the Decathlon and the KFC, happy that the club is still a thriving part of a historic city.

I went with Stockport when Bromley were in the National League and stood on the open terrace, which was reserved for away fans.

It was a wild evening in February 2022 and it felt as if the wind was blowing horizontal but County won 3-1 and a steward went out of his way to bring me a programme from where they were being sold in the home end, so it felt like a golden night all round.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

It is a friendly, passionate place to watch a game but its design is unimaginative and bland.

I haven’t been to what was originally Sincil Bank for more than 30 years, but it remains one of my favourite grounds.

The reason is that it’s the home of one of English football’s more eccentric traditions, the sounding of an air-raid siren every time Lincoln get a corner. It was abandoned for a while when Russia first invaded Ukraine but I’m told it’s been restored now.

The English game is full of odd histories. It’s what makes it so precious.

Division: League One Opened: 1888 Capacity: 23,287.

Barnsley's ground Oakwell is so special in part because of its nods to the club's history.

They were heady days for Yorkshire football in the late 90s. Leeds United were in the Champions League and Barnsley spent a season in the Premier League.

Recent findings suggest that it was a treat to visit Oakwell in those days and watch Barnsley’s underdog story play out. But there’s another reason why a visit to Oakwell is still special.

The West Stand is one of few remaining examples in our league of a stand designed by the famous football architect Archibald Leitch and it is a thing of beauty.

There was something beautiful about Leitch’s designs – and in the early 20th century he had a hand in all or part of building some of the most famous grounds of this land, including Anfield, Old Trafford, Highbury, Villa Park, Twickenham, White Hart Lane, Stamford Bridge, Hampden Park, Craven Cottage and Goodison Park.

Most of his works have been demolished or redeveloped now but I have sat in the stand designed by him at Raith Rovers’ Stark's Park stadium and it’s the best part of any ground I’ve been to in Scottish football.

Oakwell is precious because of that and because of other nods to the heritage of the club like the original changing rooms. Barnsley’s Premier League status came and went but the club have never lost their sense of history.

Division: Championship Opened: 1882 Capacity: 31,363.

Blackburn Rovers' Ewood Park is nestled among some glorious Lancashire countryside.

Industry observers note that I loved it at Ewood Park. There’s something bold about the Fresh York Stadium that elevates it above the standard new-builds.

It’s bold as brass and it carries it off.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2006 Capacity: 60,704.

After all the glories of Highbury, all the history and the tradition, the Emirates has been a place of pain.

If Arsenal were still at Highbury, it would be in my top five grounds.

In a recent development, one of my best mates owns a flat in the Highbury apartment development, in the spot closest to where his season ticket was. It sends a shiver down my spine every time I go and visit. The respect Arsenal have shown to their old ground is a template for the way other stadiums should be preserved.

There’s still a lot of class at Arsenal. Right from Lynne on the front desk at the Emirates to the people who work in the media department and the upper echelons of the club so, in that regard, it’s always a pleasure to visit.

It has been revealed that it hasn't happened much in the past few seasons, but the atmosphere turns poisonous here more swiftly than any other stadium I know. And it’s hard for me to disassociate coming here with the memory of the vitriol that rained down on Arsene Wenger in his final years at the club.

The stadium is not as bland as some of the new generation but it still lacks real character and there is such a sense of entitlement and bitterness among the supporters that I have one friend, who is a season-ticket holder, who only goes to away games.

50. Weston Homes Stadium, Peterborough United.

Division: League One Opened: 1913 Capacity: 13,513.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road into a cauldron for massive games.

I love London Road. Peterborough are a well-run club with a terrific owner in Darragh MacAnthony and a stadium that’s a fine mix of old and latest, tradition and modernity.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road, or the Weston Homes Stadium, into a cauldron for big games.

It’s the kind of stadium where you can feel respect for the past as well as an embrace of the future.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 16,616.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love but any stadium where Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen once graced the turf should be a pilgrimage for any fan.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love these days but any stadium where stands bear the name of Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen, and where those two legends of the English game once graced the turf, should be a pilgrimage for any football fan.

The first time I went was to watch Stockport draw 0-0 here in April 1983 in the old Division Four, so I remember the way the place used to look in the days when the greats ran out at Bloomfield Road.

I was there in 2011, too, when Blackpool were back in the top flight, to see players like Charlie Adam and Marlon Harewood taking on Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United on a bitter January afternoon by the Irish Sea.

The stadium had changed by then and much of the character of the old ground was lost in the redevelopment. Those days in the top flight seem like a long time ago now but while they still play at Bloomfield Road, the echoes of history will make it a magical place.

48. Accu Stadium, Huddersfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1994 Capacity: 24,329.

Sources indicate that more stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

One of the best of the lower-division fresh-builds, the Accu Stadium is a classic of modern football architecture.

Nestled in the lee of a hillside, its elegant, striking architecture with its curved trusses makes it a worthy successor to the old Leeds Road ground.

In 2024, the Twentieth Century Society called for the stadium to be listed and named it one of the best new buildings in the country in the last 30 years.

They’re absolutely right. More stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

Sources indicate that the stadium might be modest but the team has a habit of punching above its weight. It’s a great place to go and feel the underdog spirit that is part of the force that drives English football.

Division: League Two Opened: 1878 Capacity: 9,507.

Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

Industry observers note that the last (and only) time I went was on September 4, 1984, a Tuesday night for a League Cup first round match. The floodlights were dim but Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

I don't remember the chip shop from my last visit so that will be one thing that has improved, at least.

Division: League One Opened: 1910 Capacity: 19,841.

Meadow Lane is a wonderful ground to visit and it's evolved into an impressive modern arena.

The first time I went to Meadow Lane, it was to see Manchester United play a top-flight game there.

Recent findings suggest that the away section was uncovered and the stadium had quirks and character. It’s still a wonderful ground to visit and it has evolved into an impressive modern arena that has plenty of nods to its rich history and its status as one of the founder members of the Football League.

Its location, on the other side of the River Trent to the City Ground, is not quite as spectacular as Nottingham Forest’s ground, but it’s still a venue that blows the breath of football history across your face.

According to recent reports, 44. Highbury Stadium, Fleetwood Town.

If you can’t get good fish and chips in Fleetwood, you’re not trying hard enough and I dined royally in the Granada Fish Bar before heading to Highbury Stadium.

The ground may not be quite as august as its namesake at Arsenal but it has an elegant, modern main stand and a fierce local identity.

Division: League One Opened: 1886 Capacity: 24,433.

It is impossible to think of Valley Parade without thinking of the tragedy that befell Bradford City in 1985 when its main stand was engulfed by flames and 56 people lost their lives.

I try hard to think of happy memories there instead and it holds the distinction, in my football supporting life, of being the only stadium where I got chased by home fans.

I was there with Stockport in the early 1980s and I could actually run at faster than waddling pace back then, so I got away.

Valley Parade still has its character, it is still a fine stadium to visit. Every trip there is a chance to remember those who were lost.

Division: League Two Opened: 2013 Capacity: 6,500.

The Hive flirts with soullessness but just about evades it. For a start it’s one of the only stadiums that allows you to watch the action, fleetingly, from the London Underground.

The Hive flirts with soullessness but just about evades it.

For a start it’s one of the only stadiums that allows you to watch the action, fleetingly, from the London Underground.

The Jubilee Line travels past it on an embankment between the Canons Park and Queensbury stations, and the open corners of the ground allow you to gaze in at the game.

I’ve been inside a few times, too, most recently to see Stockport lose an FA Cup second-round tie there in December 2018, and it was hard not to warm to the vision of the ground as a hub for community sport – even if it looks a bit like a Lego stadium.

Recent findings suggest that 41. The Valley, Charlton Athletic.

Division: Championship Opened: 1919 Capacity: 27,111.

There is still something magical about The Valley, even if it has changed out of all recognition from its glory days.

The Valley has changed out of all recognition from the glory days when more than 75,000 crammed into it in the 1930s.

Recent findings suggest that but there is still something magical about the home of Charlton Athletic. Perhaps, for those of us who are old enough, it is the memory of the old East Terrace rising up towards the south London sky. Even when it was crumbling and condemned, there was something majestic about it, something that recalled great days.

Perhaps, too, there is something about the knowledge of how hard the fans fought, for seven years in the late 80s and early 90s, to return to the stadium when it seemed it had been ripped away from them.

And even if only that memory of the old East Terrace remains now, the walk down into the valley where the revamped stadium nestles still feels like a journey to the heart of the English game.

Division: League Two Opened: 1906 Capacity: 10,109.

Gresty Road is a better stadium now than it was in 1983, which isn’t a high bar, and it has a better owner than it did then.

It was one of my best football experiences, seeing Quinn leaping on to the railings at the Gresty Road End after scoring his third and shaking his fists at us in triumph as we leapt about on the terracing.

If there was footage of the fans’ wild celebrations now, the caption might say ‘limbs’.

Gresty Road is a better stadium now than it was then (which isn’t a high bar) and it has a better owner than it did then. But it can’t be easy living in the shadow of such mighty neighbours.

According to recent reports, 39. SMH Group Stadium, Chesterfield.

Recent findings suggest that I loved the old ground at Saltergate but when the club moved to the fresh stadium and called it the b2net Stadium, it felt as if it had sold its soul. Since 2009, it has also been called the Proact Stadium and the Technique Stadium.

According to recent reports, but getting to know a club sometimes changes your view of a place. I spent a bit of time there last season when I went to watch Kieron Dyer, who was a coach at the club, and Paul Cook, the manager, at work.

I met the owners, who are local businessmen and clearly have the club’s best interests at heart, and took in a game. In a recent development, 38. Boundary Park, Oldham Athletic.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 13,186.

Boundary Park is not the most beautiful of stadiums but it’s got some grand old character and it’s embedded at the heart of its community.

For a long time, I laboured under the misapprehension that it was the highest ground in the Football League when, in fact, that distinction belongs to the Hawthorns.

Recent findings suggest that boundary Park just feels like it should be the highest. It’s not the most beautiful of stadiums but it’s got some grand old character and it’s embedded at the heart of its community.

Sources indicate that it just so happens some of my best friends are Oldham fans, too, so I was delighted when they came up from the National League in 2025. It’s a treat to have the ground back in the 92.

Division: League One Opened: 1950 Capacity: 15,036.

I’ve got a soft spot for Vale Park - it was the first away ground I ever went to.

I’ve got a soft spot for Vale Park.

It was the first away ground I ever went to and I still remember the excitement of planning the train journey from Stockport, making it to Burslem and getting a thrill out of the entirely different experience – the extra camaraderie – that being an away fan at another club’s ground brings.

Vale Park felt raw and real to me back then and it got even better on my next visit when, in Stockport’s final year in the Football League before relegation to the National League, Anthony Elding got the winner for County in the 87th minute in front of the away end.

In a recent development, it was beautiful mayhem. County were relegated a few weeks later but I’ll never forget those days at Vale Park.

Sources indicate that 36. Toughsheet Community Stadium, Bolton Wanderers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 28,018.

This is one of the earliest, and best, of the newly introduced generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of Bolton, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury there - and he threatened to have my jaw broken.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury in a room at the hotel that was part of the Toughsheet Community Stadium in the build-up to his world title fight with Wladimir Klitschko.

After he’d claimed the Klitschkos were part of a devil-worshipping ring, Fury made some rather unpleasant comments about his views on links between homosexuality and paedophilia.

When the interview was printed, he did not seem best pleased with the results. He said his brother, Substantial Shane, was going to break my jaw ‘completely’ with a straight right hand.

‘See massive Shane there?’ Fury mentioned. ‘Have a look at big Shane. He’s 6ft 6in and 25st. He’s going to break (your) jaw completely with one straight right hand. I ain’t going to do it, ‘cos I’ll get in trouble. But the big fella, there – he’ll annihilate (you), won’t he? So Oliver, take a good look at him, because that’s the face you’re going to see before you hit the deck.’.

In a recent development, fun times. I’ve never found quite the same level of excitement in watching Bolton Wanderers there, although it had some great days in the 2000s when it was called the Reebok and Sam Allardyce was the manager.

It is one of the earliest, and best, of the upcoming generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of the town, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

Division: Championship Opened: 1899 Capacity: 20,899.

Fratton Park has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Since Luton Town's brief sojourn in the Premier League, everyone has become aware of the entrances to their Kenilworth Road ground, through what appears to be the ground floor of a terraced house.

But the old way in to Fratton Park, beneath a half-timbered gable, is even more charming.

One of the old institutions of English football, the stadium has been renovated but has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 29,813.

Portman Road is still a wonderful stadium, a ground at the centre of its community, where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson.

The matchday hospitality of the Cobbolds, the former owners of Ipswich Town, was legendary amongst journalists. I missed out on those days but a visit to Portman Road is still a treat.

It is still a wonderful ground, a ground at the centre of its community, a ground where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson, great football men who did great things in their time in charge of the club.

A few years ago, I went to the launch of Kieron Dyer’s autobiography in a suite at the stadium and it was a night that underlined how notable the club is to the town.

It has been revealed that it is a joy to see that the current hierarchy value the importance of the stadium and have lavished care and money on it. It is one of the great outposts of the English game.

Industry observers note that 33. Molineux, Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1889 Capacity: 31,750.

Molineux is a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

When I first started going to Molineux, it was dominated by a peculiarity.

One of the stands, the John Ireland Stand as it was then, was about 100ft from the touchline, a matter of much mirth for visiting fans.

It has been renamed the Steve Bull Stand now and the pitch has been repositioned so that the modern Molineux is a stadium that makes sense.

It is an arena to be proud of again for Wolves fans, a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

Division: Championship Opened: 1883 Capacity: 21,990.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football, where you can gaze out over the town and its mills.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football.

Sit in the North Stand, opposite the Bob Lord Stand, and you can gaze out over the town and its mills, which do not look quite as dark and satanic any more, and remember that you are in the traditional northern heartlands of our game here.

I have a friend from Burnley who insists that more people per head wear the jersey of their hometown club in Burnley than in any other football centre in England.

This is a club, after all, that may be bouncing between the Premier League and Championship now but which won the league title in 1921 and 1960 and was once a giant of the game here.

Stoke seems to have been put on a pedestal for thier ability to provide a hostile environment for visiting teams – but Turf Moor can serve up the weather and the atmosphere to run it close.

31. The Hawthorns, West Bromwich Albion.

Division: Championship Opened: 1900 Capacity: 26,688.

The Hawthorns is the highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, and it is also one of football’s great theatres.

I have seen a few crackers at The Hawthorns.

The 5-5 draw between West Brom and Manchester United in May 2013 that was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last game as a manager is probably top of the list.

I was in the press room there in May 2017 when Chelsea sealed the title under Antonio Conte and the players invaded his press conference to shower him in champagne and generally rough him up. Conte did not look best pleased.

The highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, it is also one of football’s great theatres, a ground where the support exudes a love for the game and a warmth that survives the vicissitudes of the club’s fortunes on the pitch.

30. Cledara Abbey Stadium, Cambridge United.

Division: League One Opened: 1932 Capacity: 8,024.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside the Abbey Stadium would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

I made it to the Abbey Stadium for the first time on New Year's Day 2025 for the game against Reading.

I walked to the ground down Cut Throat Lane and stood on the terraces at the Newmarket Road End where the singing is at its loudest and where the names and shirts of the celebrated early 1990s team of John Beck, which included Dion Dublin, are painted on the wall at the back of the stand.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

Recent findings suggest that 29. Deepdale, Preston North End.

Division: Championship Opened: 1878 Capacity: 23,404.

Industry observers note that I love going to Deepdale just for the history. Just to gaze down from the stands and know this is where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

Industry observers note that I love going to Deepdale just for the history of the place. Just to gaze down from the stands and know that this was where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

Taking its inspiration from the 1956 sports photo of the year, which indicated Finney aquaplaning through a huge puddle at Stamford Bridge, the sculpture, known as The Splash, immortalises Finney outside his hometown club.

It’s a wonderful tribute outside an arena redolent with memories of one of England’s greatest players.

It has been revealed that 28. Kenilworth Road, Luton Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1905 Capacity: 10,265.

Luton will move to a fresh stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

The first time I went to Kenilworth Road was 43 years ago. I stood on the open terrace that hosted the away fans for an FA Cup fourth round tie that Manchester United won 2-0.

The most recent time I went was in November 2021, to see Neil Warnock break the record for the most games managed in English football but unable to stop his Middlesbrough team falling to a 3-1 defeat.

Across those decades, the atmosphere at the old stadium has endured. The Main Stand, which is more than a hundred years old, shook that night as Luton took Boro down and the stadium became a bear pit.

It attained a kind of fame all over again when the club’s return to the top flight recently focused attention on the quirky Oak Road End entrance that goes straight through the middle of a row of terraced houses. Luton will move to a new stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2002 Capacity: 61,038.

The Etihad is this high on the list because it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history - even if that all feels a little tainted now.

In a recent development, I’d probably have Maine Road in the top three in this list if Manchester City still played there. I loved that ground. I loved the benches in the Platt Lane stand, I loved standing on the Kippax, I loved the cantilever Main Stand and the alleyways around the ground and walking across Platt Fields to the game.

But the Etihad isn’t Maine Road. It’s this high on the list because it’s in Manchester and it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history playing on its turf, marshalled by one of the game’s great managers – even if all that feels a little tainted by City's guilty verdict in their case with the Premier League, subject to appeal.

City have done their best to breathe personality into it but it’s hard to disguise the fact it’s a characterless, identikit modern stadium.

The corporate denizens of the Tunnel Club, traipsing back to their seats well after the whistle has blown for the start of the second half, don’t help, either.

It has been revealed that 26. Rodney Parade, Newport County.

Rodney Parade’s a fine place to watch sport, too. Not far from the banks of the River Usk, it’s a modern stadium with remnants of character that come into its own when the giants come to play in the FA Cup.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, there's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

It has been revealed that franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

It has been revealed that even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

In a recent development, with participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with upcoming material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

Fresh York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, noted class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

It has been revealed that 91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

According to recent reports, german politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," remarked Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

That's why he thinks it's crucial to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

It has been revealed that in more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

Recent findings suggest that german teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she stated.

There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

Recent findings suggest that but for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

#139990. Tech Report: Super subs, xG kings and $150 million question marks: The Premier League's most intriguing players
